strengths: Principled theoretical approach using null-space projection with formal mathematical proofs and clear motivation over heuristic baselines
Strong empirical results with ~90%+ average DSR across three models and seven jailbreak attacks while maintaining utility comparable to vanilla models
Comprehensive experimental evaluation covering three different LLM architectures, diverse jailbreak attacks, multiple utility benchmarks, and strong comparisons with three baselines
Excellent visualization and analysis of activation dynamics, demonstrating clear separation between benign and malicious steering patterns
Practical efficiency with inference-time steering requiring no post-training; clear implementation details and reproducibility support
Thorough experimental appendices with extensive ablations, L2 norm analysis, eigenvalue distributions, and multiple case studies
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: adapts well-established null-space projection techniques from prior work (AlphaEdit, continual learning) to activation steering rather than developing fundamentally new theory

Insufficient theoretical justification for key assumptions: why benign activations should reliably enable null-space-constrained steering is assumed but not proven; no convergence guarantees or formal failure mode analysis

Heavy hyperparameter tuning dependency: different λ values required per model (0.5/0.45/0.14), arbitrary p% threshold selection, and no principled guidance for new models undermines generalizability claims

Limited evaluation scope: only 7B-9B models tested (no larger or smaller models), relatively small test set (100 questions), only 7 jailbreak attacks, no adaptive attack evaluation, and no statistical rigor (no confidence intervals or significance tests)

Incomplete ablations: RV baseline comparison is a strawman (100% DSR but destroys utility); missing separation of contributions from null-space projection vs. learned refusal reconstruction; unclear sensitivity to Hb coverage and Dr/Dc quality

Underexplored dependency on refusal vector quality: performance relies on difference-in-means extraction but limited analysis of robustness to r quality, extraction dataset composition, or update strategies
Missing robustness analysis: no evaluation against adaptive attacks aware of AlphaSteer's mechanism, no out-of-distribution generalization testing, and no transferability assessment across models
Practical limitations acknowledged but unaddressed: requires access to internal activations limiting deployment; only linear matrices explored; acknowledged but not tested on different model sizes

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing the practical safety-utility trade-off in activation steering
Mathematically formalized approach using null-space projection theory with detailed proofs
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 3 models, 7 jailbreak attacks, and 4 utility benchmarks
Effective visualizations (PCA plots, activation dynamics) that provide mechanistic insights
Strong empirical results maintaining utility while achieving 91-98% DSR across models
Extensive appendices with implementation details and supplementary analyses
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty—primarily applies existing null-space projection techniques (well-established in continual learning and knowledge editing) to activation steering without significant innovation
Weak theoretical justification: core assumption that null-space steering preserves utility is purely empirical, not theoretically grounded despite claims of being 'principled'
Misleading safety-utility comparison: RV baseline achieves 100% DSR vs AlphaSteer's 91.93%, yet paper claims AlphaSteer 'outperforms' it; this is a trade-off, not dominance
Hyperparameter selection appears ad-hoc (p%=0.6, α=10, layer selection via visual inspection of Figure D.6) with no principled procedure or ablations on α and p%
Data imbalance in training: benign activations (14K prompts) vs malicious (2K prompts); refusal vector from only 720 prompts; no sensitivity analysis
DSR evaluation uses GPT-4o as classifier introducing circular dependency; only 100 test prompts per attack type without reported confidence intervals or significance tests
Code availability link is missing/blank; layer selection procedure unclear and dataset-dependent; no principled per-model hyperparameter selection procedure
No analysis of failure modes: why does Cipher attack yield only 63% DSR for Llama but near-100% for other models/attacks? No adversarial robustness analysis against null-space-targeted attacks
Limited baseline comparisons: RV is the method's own vector (unfair), and recent safety methods (sparse autoencoders, knowledge editing approaches) are cited but not experimentally compared
Generalization questions unaddressed: how sensitive is null-space learned from one benign dataset to novel benign prompts? No transfer analysis

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear solution: The paper identifies heuristic limitations in prior activation steering work and proposes principled null-space projection approach
Sound theoretical framework: Lemma 1 is correctly proven, closed-form solution properly derived, mathematical presentation is rigorous
Comprehensive and convincing experimental evaluation: Three models, seven jailbreak attacks, multiple utility benchmarks with proper train/test separation and data deduplication

Strong consistent empirical results: AlphaSteer achieves ~91.93% avg DSR (vs. Surgical's 82.83%) while maintaining utility at 67.3% (vs. Surgical's 59.3%), demonstrating genuine safety-utility balance
Excellent presentation and reproducibility: Clear motivation with intuitive visualizations (Figure 1c), comprehensive appendices, implementation details provided, code promised
Effective visualization of activation dynamics: Figure 3 clearly shows benign activations remain stable while malicious ones shift toward refusal, validating the approach
Practical solution to a real safety problem: Better balance than both vector calibration (heuristic) and conditional steering (manual thresholding)
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: Applies existing null-space projection techniques (from AlphaEdit, continual learning) to activation steering; contribution is primarily in application rather than methodological innovation

Gap between theory and practice: Requires p%=0.6 eigenvalue threshold for practical implementation, undermining theoretical guarantees; lacks principled justification or sensitivity analysis for this critical hyperparameter

Unclear attribution of improvements: RV baseline (direct steering with AlphaSteer's refusal vector) achieves 99%+ DSR compared to AlphaSteer's 91.93%; insufficient ablation studies isolating contributions of: (a) learned transformation matrix Δ, (b) null-space constraint, (c) linear regression formulation

Incomplete technical analysis: Regularization coefficient α lacks principled selection; missing analysis of why forcing small steering norms for benign prompts automatically works for malicious prompts; no ablation testing null-space constraint applied to baseline methods

Practical deployment concerns underexplored: Requires maintaining 14,000 benign prompts for null-space computation; layer selection is post-hoc based on test data separability; computational overhead at inference not discussed; unknown robustness to benign distribution shift

Limited evaluation scope: Only three models (all open-source instruction-tuned); model size scaling effects unexplored per authors' acknowledgment; only linear transformations tested despite mentioning MLPs as potential extension

Theoretical grounding overstated: Claims of being 'theoretically grounded' are weakened by practical approximations (p% threshold) that violate theoretical assumptions; missing generalization or robustness guarantees

Evaluation methodology issues: GPT-4o-based classification introduces potential bias; DSR metric is binary (doesn't capture refusal quality); some baseline results surprisingly poor (CAST fails all math tasks)—unclear if fair implementation

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear articulation of limitations in existing approaches
Principled null-space constraint framework with formal mathematical grounding and proofs
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 3 models, 7 jailbreaks, and 4 utility benchmarks
Consistent and substantial improvements over multiple baselines (average 91.93% DSR vs baselines ~80-85%)
Excellent reproducibility with public code, detailed implementation, and extensive appendices
Robust to adaptive white-box GCG attacks (95.5% DSR), demonstrating genuine robustness
Clear visualization of activation dynamics and intuitive geometric interpretation
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—applies existing null-space projection technique (Wang et al. 2021, Fang et al. 2025) to activation steering without significant methodological innovation
Incomplete solution to stated problem: still exhibits safety-utility trade-off (Gemma drops from 63.8% to 62.4% utility), requires 14K benign samples for optimal performance
Strong but unvalidated assumption that malicious activation→refusal direction mapping is linear (Eq. 7); failure modes when assumption breaks unexplored
Practical dependency on benign activation space coverage: utility score collapses to 39.43% with 1K samples (Table 14); unclear how to handle out-of-distribution benign behaviors
Evaluation relies heavily on single GPT-4o judge; Figure 24 reveals evaluation mismatches (Llama-Guard mistakes jailbreaks); no reasoning model evaluation despite their increasing deployment
Hyperparameter sensitivity and non-principled tuning: model-specific λ values (0.5/0.45/0.14) without clear selection procedure; DSR varies 81.80%-98.80% with p% (Tables 16-17)
Failure case analysis missing: Cipher achieves only 63% DSR with limited discussion of attack robustness variability; no analysis of overlapping malicious/benign subspaces
Generalization concerns: built on single-direction refusal assumption (questioned by concurrent work on concept cones); effectiveness on frontier models untested

strengths: Addresses well-motivated problem of safety-utility tradeoff in LLM activation steering with clear practical motivation
Theoretically grounded approach using null-space projection with formal definitions and correct proofs (Lemmas 1-2)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 7 jailbreak attacks, 4 utility benchmarks, and 3 model architectures with extensive ablations
Strong empirical results: 91.93% average DSR while maintaining 67.3% utility score, consistently outperforming multiple baselines
Effective visualizations (PCA, L2 norm distributions) that clearly demonstrate activation dynamics and learned behavior
Good reproducibility: detailed implementation specifications, comprehensive appendices, promised code release
Robust evaluation including adaptive white-box attacks, generalization tests, and space coverage analysis
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: core contribution applies existing null-space projection techniques from knowledge editing (Fang et al., 2025) to activation steering without significant algorithmic innovation
Critical theoretical gap: no explanation for why benign activations should naturally align with a meaningful null-space; paper only shows empirical success without mechanistic understanding
Strong dependence on benign data coverage (Table 14): utility drops from 67.3% to 39.43% with reduced data; no principled method to determine sufficient coverage
Hyperparameter sensitivity without guidance: p% parameter causes 81.8%-98.8% DSR variance and different values needed per model; no principled selection process for practitioners
Limited model scale: only 8B-9B models tested; effectiveness on larger models (13B+, reasoning models) explicitly stated as unknown in limitations
Evaluation methodology concerns: reliance on proprietary GPT-4o for DSR assessment; Appendix G shows dramatic differences with Llama-Guard-3-8B; single adaptive attack insufficient
Incomplete white-box security analysis: only one adaptive attack tested; sophisticated attackers could target null-space structure directly
Weak limitations discussion: Section 5 is extremely brief and vague about data requirements, hyperparameter selection, computational overhead, and theoretical gaps

strengths: Clear problem motivation with compelling visualization of safety-utility trade-off in prior methods
Novel theoretical approach: null-space projection is principled, elegant, and computationally efficient (Lemma 1)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 3 models × 7 jailbreaks × 4 utility benchmarks with rigorous ablations
Outstanding empirical results: consistently achieves ~92% DSR while maintaining baseline utility, while baselines show degradation
Excellent mechanistic understanding: PCA visualizations, L2 norm distributions, and activation shift analysis clearly demonstrate how method works
Strong reproducibility: public code, detailed implementation details, hyperparameter justification, data deduplication verification
Consistent performance across models and attacks demonstrates robustness and generalization
Well-positioned relative to related work with clear categorization of prior heuristic approaches
weaknesses: Limitations section is underdeveloped: fails to discuss fundamental constraints (space coverage dependency only in appendix, when benign/malicious separability fails, no failure mode analysis)
Space coverage as critical hidden dependency: Table 14 shows utility drops from 67.3% to 39.43% with less benign data; no principled guidance for required data size
Hyperparameter sensitivity under-addressed: p% shows large sensitivity, different λ per model, no principled selection method beyond empirical tuning
O(D²) inference-time overhead (13× vs Surgical/CAST) claimed negligible; for D=4096 this is ~16M operations/layer with no runtime comparisons
Evaluation limitations: relies on GPT-4o with known biases (Appendix G shows Cipher DSR 0→100% with Llama-Guard), only 100 test prompts, binary DSR metric misses nuanced failures
Cipher attack shows notably lower performance (63%); no systematic investigation of failure modes or attack characteristics causing degradation
Limited robustness analysis: adaptive GCG only 200 steps, mechanism of why dynamic steering helps not deeply analyzed, recent jailbreaks not evaluated
Contribution is somewhat incremental: improves steering paradigm rather than fundamentally advancing LLM safety; inference-time approach has inherent limitations vs training-time methods
